children.value: Check Your Understanding: Interpreting the Test Statistic

children.label: Check Your Understanding: Interpreting the Test Statistic

model.question: In the death penalty example, the test statistic was $z = 2.31$. Which is the correct interpretation of this value?

choices.text: The sample proportion is 2.31 standard deviations above the null value, assuming $H_0$ is true
choices.feedback: Correct! Assuming $H_0$ is true (p = 0.64), the observed sample proportion 0.675 lies 2.31 standard deviations above the null value.

choices.text: The sample proportion is 2.31 percentage points above the null value
choices.feedback: The test statistic is measured in standard deviations, not percentage points.

choices.text: There is a 2.31% chance that $H_0$ is true
choices.feedback: z is not a probability—the p-value (a probability) will be derived from it in the next step.

model.hint: A z-score counts standard deviations from the center of the null distribution.

children.value: Check Your Understanding: The Test Statistic in Context

children.label: Check Your Understanding: The Test Statistic in Context

children.value: The UCLA Internet Report (February 2003) estimated that a proportion of roughly 0.75 of online homes were still using dial-up access, but claimed that the use of dial-up was declining. To examine this, a follow-up study was conducted a year later in which, out of a random sample of 1,308 households that had Internet access, 804 were connecting using a dial-up modem.
Let p be the proportion of all U.S. Internet-using households that have dial-up access. In the previous activity, we established that the appropriate hypotheses here are

children.html: H0:p=0.75H_0: p = 0.75H0​:p=0.75
Ha:p<0.75H_a: p < 0.75Ha​:p<0.75

model.question: What is the sample proportion p-hat in this study?

choices.feedback: 0.75 is the null value from the earlier report, not the sample result.
Divide the number of dial-up households by the total sample size.

model.question: The test statistic for these data is approximately $z = -11.3$. What does this value tell us?

choices.text: The sample proportion is 11.3 standard deviations below 0.75—extremely strong evidence that dial-up use declined
choices.feedback: Correct! The sample proportion is more than 11 standard deviations BELOW 0.75—essentially impossible if $H_0$ were true—so the data provide overwhelming evidence that dial-up use declined.

choices.text: The negative sign means the test was done incorrectly
choices.feedback: A negative z simply means p-hat is below the null value—which is exactly the direction the alternative predicts.

choices.text: The evidence against $H_0$ is weak because z is negative
choices.feedback: The magnitude matters: 11.3 standard deviations is an enormous discrepancy, providing extremely strong evidence against $H_0$.

model.hint: How surprising is a sample proportion more than 11 standard deviations below the null value?

children.value: Ann and Sam are both testing the hypothesis that 40% of plain M&M’s are orange,

children.html: H0:p=0.40H_0: p = 0.40H0​:p=0.40

children.value: . Ann draws a sample of M&M’s and 45% of her sample are orange; she calculates a test statistic of

children.html: z=1.25z = 1.25z=1.25

children.value: . Sam draws a sample of M&M’s and 50% of his sample are orange; he calculates a test statistic of

children.html: z=1z = 1z=1

model.question: Which of the following statements are true? (Select all that apply.)

choices.text: Ann's data provide stronger evidence against $H_0$ than Sam's, because her test statistic is larger
choices.feedback: True! Evidence is measured by the test statistic, and Ann's |z| = 1.25 exceeds Sam's |z| = 1.

choices.text: Sam's sample must be smaller than Ann's
choices.feedback: True! Sam's difference (0.10) is larger than Ann's (0.05), yet his z is smaller—so his standard error must be larger, meaning his sample was smaller.

choices.text: Sam's data provide stronger evidence against $H_0$, because his sample proportion is farther from 0.40
choices.feedback: False—raw distance from the null value doesn't determine evidence strength; the standardized distance does.

choices.text: Both results confirm that exactly 40% of plain M&M's are orange
choices.feedback: False—both test statistics are positive and neither is large, so neither sample gives strong evidence; and in any case a test never proves that $H_0$ is true.

model.hint: The test statistic already accounts for sample size—compare the z values, not the raw percentages. And if Sam's larger difference gave a SMALLER z, what must be true of his standard error?
